title: T1595.003 — Active Scanning - Wordlist Scanning
subtitle: Watch a directory wordlist scan against a company website: mostly misses, then two painful finds.
aria: Simulation. Step 1: Load the wordlist. The attacker loads a wordlist: thousands of likely names for hidden files and folders. Wordlist scanning is simply trying each name against the website.

steps.title: Load the wordlist
steps.caption: The attacker loads a wordlist: thousands of likely names for hidden files and folders. Wordlist scanning is simply trying each name against the website.
steps.defender: These lists are public and free, so assume every common name is being tried against your site every day, by many sources.

detection.label: No detection
detection.detail: This activity is not visible to the victim yet.

steps.title: Try common paths
steps.caption: The scanner requests name after name. Most answers are 404, which means not found. Each request is tiny, but thousands of them form a clear pattern.
steps.defender: A long run of 404 answers from one source is the signature of this technique. One or two 404s are browsing; hundreds per minute are a wordlist.

steps.title: A backup appears
steps.caption: The wordlist contains backup.zip and the server answers 200 OK. The attacker just found a database backup sitting in the web root.
steps.defender: Alert on 200 answers for sensitive paths: .zip, .sql, .bak, .git, .env. These should never exist in a public web root, so one hit is worth investigating.

steps.title: Source code exposed
steps.caption: The scanner also finds an exposed .git folder. That folder can contain the whole source code history, including passwords that were once committed.
steps.defender: An exposed .git or .env file is a critical finding. Treat any download of it as a secret-leak incident, not a web nuisance.

steps.title: Download everything
steps.caption: The attacker downloads the backup and the source history. The recon step is over; the data itself now gives the attacker usernames, hashes, and configuration secrets.
steps.defender: Watch egress from web servers. Large outbound transfers right after probing starts mean the attacker found and is taking something.

steps.title: WAF fights back
steps.caption: The web application firewall starts rate-limiting and returns 429 answers. The scan slows down, but the important files are already gone.
steps.defender: Rate limiting is containment, not prevention. It reduces noise and cost, but detection should fire long before the WAF becomes the only defense.

detection.label: Partial signal
detection.detail: A weak signal exists but is not yet a confirmed alert.

steps.title: Attacker switches source
steps.caption: The attacker continues from a new IP address with the same wordlist. Blocking single addresses barely matters when the pattern is what matters.
steps.defender: Tune detections on behavior - 404 bursts, sensitive-path hits, egress spikes - so a rotated source changes nothing for your alerts.

detection.label: Alert raised
detection.detail: The SOC has enough evidence to open an incident.

steps.title: Fix the root cause
steps.caption: The team removes the backup and the .git folder from the server, rotates every secret inside them, and adds alerts for this exact pattern. The attack surface is gone.
steps.defender: Fix the cause, not the symptom: build a deployment process that cannot ship backups or repositories, and verify with your own monthly wordlist scan in the lab.
